summary: For ages 6–7, germination is a procedural, observational topic: the learner grows a real plant, keeps a dated record of slow change, and comes to understand the hidden underground sequence — seed takes in water and swells → root grows DOWN first → shoot pushes UP → first leaves open → mature plant. The decisive teaching move is to reveal the normally hidden underground stage (grow a bean against the glass of a clear jar or on damp paper, or a bulb in a glass) and to contrast a seed's start with a bulb's start, with each growing into a mature plant from a different beginning. Geotropism (root heads down whichever way the seed is placed) anchors that the sequence is directional, not random.
misconceptions: Thinking the shoot comes up first / the whole plant pushes up together — many children don't know the ROOT emerges first and grows downward.
Believing a seed needs soil to germinate — seeds germinate on damp paper; they need water and warmth, not soil, to start (soil/light matter later for growth).
Assuming a seed needs light to germinate — most seeds germinate in the dark; light becomes essential once leaves form.
Thinking a bigger seed always grows into a bigger/faster plant.
Not recognising a bulb as a plant start at all (seeing it as just an onion-like object rather than a stored-food beginning).

activities.title: Grow-a-bean against the glass: watch the hidden underground sequence
steps: Place a bean seed against the inside wall of a clear jar, held there by damp paper or cotton wool so the underground part stays visible; keep the paper moist and the jar in a warm place.

Over about a week (timing varies with warmth and seed type), look each day and notice the order of what appears: typically the seed swells with water, then a root emerges and grows DOWNWARD, then a shoot pushes UPWARD, then the first leaves open.
Name each stage aloud or label it as it appears: 'seed drinks and swells → root grows down → shoot grows up → leaves open'.
Set up a second jar with the bean placed a different way up (e.g. upside down) and watch whether the root still turns to grow downward.

Grow a bulb in a glass alongside, with its base just touching the water rather than sitting under it (a bulb under water can rot), and compare how its start differs from the seed's — each grows into a mature plant from a different beginning.
activities.insight: In this bean example, the root emerges before the shoot and usually grows downward while the shoot grows upward. The clear jar reveals stages normally hidden underground. A bulb begins differently, with an existing bud and food-storing tissues; compare what each actual plant does.

activities.title: Dated observation diary of a growing plant
steps: Each day for about a week, draw and label what you can see of the growing plant in a dated box (day 1, day 2, day 3 and so on).
Add words to each drawing describing what is new that day (seed swollen, root down, shoot up, first leaves).
At the end, lay the dated drawings in order and describe how the plant changed step by step, saying which part appeared first.
If you also have mixed-up picture cards of a germinating seed, arrange them to match the order you actually observed and explain your ordering.
activities.insight: Slow change becomes a comparable, orderable sequence when it is recorded over time; careful dated recording is itself the core science skill here, not an add-on.

activities.title: Seed versus bulb: two starts, each into a mature plant
steps: Look closely at a seed and a bulb side by side, and predict how each will begin to grow.

Watch (or recall from your growing records) how each one begins: the seed first swells and pushes out a root, while the bulb grows roots from its base and a shoot from the bud already inside it. Note which one you actually saw grow faster.
Carefully cut a bulb open with adult help (do not eat it and wash hands afterwards) to see the tiny leaves/plant and the stored food already inside, and notice the flat base where roots grow from.

Explain that both starts contain a young plant and stored food. A seed has an embryo protected by a seed coat; a bulb has an existing bud with thick food-storing leaves around a short stem. Observe the different starts without claiming every bulb grows faster than every seed.
activities.insight: Seeds and bulbs are different plant starting structures; both can contain a young plant and food reserves. Each can develop into a mature plant, with the observed timing depending on the specimen and conditions.

activities.title: What does a seed actually need to start?
steps: Set up cress or bean seeds on damp cotton wool or paper with NO soil, and keep them warm and moist.
Predict whether they will sprout without soil, then watch what happens over several days.
With adult help, try placing one damp set in a dark cupboard and, over several days, notice whether the seeds still begin to sprout there.

Describe what these bean or cress seeds received to begin growing: water, oxygen from air, and a suitable temperature. They used stored food. Light requirements differ among species; use the observed examples rather than claiming all seeds germinate in darkness. Growing seedlings later need light for photosynthesis and a suitable supply of water and nutrients.
activities.insight: These seeds can germinate without soil because they have food reserves, provided water, oxygen and suitable temperature are available. Their dark-germination result is an observation about the chosen species and conditions, not a universal rule for all seeds.

activities.title: Order the germination stages and check your understanding
steps: Put the stages of germination in the correct order: swollen seed → root grows down → shoot grows up → first leaves open → mature plant.
Answer: which part of the plant appears first? (the root)
Match a seed's starting point and a bulb's starting point to how each one begins to grow.
Explain why the root growing first and downward makes sense (it anchors the plant and takes in water).
activities.insight: The learner can reliably recall and reason about the ordered, directional sequence and distinguish seed and bulb starts.

activities.title: Optional underground time-lapse model
steps: In a labelled cross-section model, add water to a seed and advance an explicitly compressed timeline to observe swelling, root emergence, shoot growth and leaves for the represented species.
Scrub back and forward and read a stage label at each step; rotate the starting seed to explore the modelled downward root response.
Run a bulb in a second lane for comparison, then compare the model’s sequence with the actual jar records rather than treating the animation as experimental proof.
activities.insight: A time-compressed cutaway can make hidden structures and the order of a represented growth sequence visible. Real observations check how well the simplified model matches the plants grown.

checkQuestion: Here are cress seeds, damp cotton wool in a clear pot, and a growing diary. Plant them and, each day for a week, draw and label what you can see. At the end, take these mixed-up picture cards of a germinating seed and put them in the order they really happened — and tell me what appeared first.
checkAnswer: The child plants the seeds, makes dated daily observational drawings, and orders the sequence correctly: seed swells as it takes in water → root grows down first → shoot pushes up → first leaves open. They note the root came before the green shoot.
